title: Land Preparation in the Philippines: A Guide for Every Crop
metaTitle: Land Preparation in the Philippines: Steps for Every Crop
metaDescription: Land preparation in the Philippines step by step: clearing, plowing, harrowing, leveling, beds and ridges, tillage machines and timing before planting.
excerpt: Land preparation in the Philippines is the work you do on a field before the first seed or seedling goes in. It decides how well water moves, how many weeds come up and how evenly the crop grows. This guide covers the basic operations, the machines, the timing before planting and a table that sends each crop to its own guide.

heroImage.alt: A tractor working a field during land preparation in the Philippines

blocks.text: Why land preparation in the Philippines decides the crop

A good seed cannot make up for a bad field. PhilRice says a poorly prepared rice field could yield 5 percent less. It also says that proper leveling solves more than 50 percent of the problems in rice production, because it helps water management, weed control and snail control.

Money follows the same rule. PhilRice estimates that proper land leveling can save about 1,850 pesos per hectare in expenses. So the weeks before planting are not lost time. They are the cheapest part of the season to get right.
Every crop uses a mix of the same few jobs. What changes is how deep, how fine and how wet the soil should be. Here is the usual order.

items.title: Clear the field and handle residue
items.text: Remove or cut the old crop, trash and weeds. For rice, clean and repair the dikes (pilapil) and ditches too. PhilRice says clean dikes cut pest buildup and compacted dikes stop seepage.

items.title: Plow
items.text: Plowing breaks and turns the soil and buries stubble and weeds. For rice, PhilRice advises plowing or rotovating 21 to 30 days before planting. For corn, the DA Cagayan Valley guide says to plow 15 to 20 cm deep when the soil moisture is right.

items.title: Harrow
items.text: Harrowing breaks clods and starts the leveling. In the PalayCheck schedule, you harrow every 7 days after plowing. The first pass follows the plowing pattern and the second goes crosswise.

items.title: Level
items.text: In rice, level the field with 5 cm of water and a wooden plank or a tiller attached leveler. In upland fields, level so that water does not pond in low spots.

items.title: Puddle (lowland rice only)
items.text: Puddling works the soil under water into soft mud. PhilRice counts a well puddled field as part of a well leveled field. Dry land crops skip this step.

items.title: Make beds, ridges, furrows or holes
items.text: Upland crops are planted in rows. For corn, the DA Cagayan Valley guide sets furrows 70 to 75 cm apart. Sugarcane furrows are about one meter apart in the Tarlac Mill District Office guide.

blocks.text: Tillage machines: carabao, hand tractor and four wheel tractor

Most Filipino farms are small, so the machine follows the farm size and the crop. A UN CSAM review of Philippine mechanization says the carabao with a single native moldboard plow is still the main draft animal for rice and corn land preparation. It adds that two wheel tractors, which we call the hand tractor, are used more each year, while sugarcane plantations use four wheel tractors.

blocks.text:
PhilRice has also built tools for hard conditions. Its Laboy Tiller works in soft, deep mud with long stubble, and its Microtiller works in fields with knee deep hard pans. A ride on attachment lets the hand tractor operator sit while plowing, harrowing and leveling, which lowers the operator's heart rate by about 10 beats per minute.

PhilMech has delivered four wheel tractors to farmer cooperatives, for example in Leyte. If you farm with a group, ask your municipal agriculture office and PhilMech about machines and custom hire. For laser guided leveling, PhilRice ran a 16 day demonstration on 10 hectares in Alaminos, Pangasinan.

PhilRice recommends a field preparation period of 21 days for rice, with plowing and harrowing once a week for three rounds before the final leveling. The weekly gap lets weeds and dropped seeds sprout so the next pass kills them. For corn, the DA Cagayan Valley guide also says to harrow two to three times with a one week interval for weed control.

Crack plowing is a shallow dry tillage that PhilRice recommends after harvest or at the start of the rainy season, so the field is already worked before the main plowing.

blocks.title: The days are counted back from planting
blocks.text: The schedule above follows the PhilRice 21 to 30 day window and the weekly harrowing rhythm. Adjust it to your soil and water supply, and ask your technician when the dry spell is long.

blocks.title: Put land preparation on the calendar
blocks.text: On anee.io, every land preparation day goes on the cropping calendar, dated back from planting. Set the planting date of a lot and the plowing, harrowing and leveling days line up behind it.
blocks.label: See the cropping calendar

blocks.text:
Minimum tillage disturbs the soil less. Zero tillage plants straight into the old stubble. In both systems, farmers usually control the standing weeds with a non selective herbicide such as glyphosate, and you must follow the FPA label.

Research in Bukidnon in 1995 compared zero tillage, minimum tillage and the usual farmer practice in corn using glyphosate plus ammonium sulphate. Corn yield matched or beat the conventional method, and the system saved cost and time. The DA Cagayan Valley guide also lists zero to minimum tillage among the soil conservation practices for hilly corn areas.

Still, these systems do not suit every field. A field that needs leveling, or one that has a hard pan, needs real tillage first.

Heavy clay needs more passes than sandy or loam soil, and it is easier to work at the right moisture. The Tarlac Mill District Office says the number of plowing and harrowing rounds for sugarcane depends on soil type, with clay needing more than light sandy loam. Acid soil needs agricultural lime first, so read our guide on [acidic soil preparation](/land-preparation/acidic-soil-preparation).

Sodic or alkaline soil and saline soil each have their own fixes. See [sodic and alkaline soil preparation](/land-preparation/sodic-alkaline-soil-preparation) and [saline soil preparation](/land-preparation/saline-soil-preparation) before you plant.

items: Plowing once and planting the next day, so the weeds that sprout later beat the crop.
Leveling without water in rice, which hides the high and low spots until it is too late.
Skipping the dike and ditch repair, which leaves rat holes and seepage.
Working clay when it is too wet or too dry, which makes clods.
Ignoring soil pH, so lime and fertilizer are wasted on acid soil.

blocks.text: Besides the calendar, you can ask Anee, the [AI technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician), what to do in Tagalog or English. Anee reads your lot, your crop and the week's weather before answering.

items.q: How many days before planting should I plow?
items.a: For rice, PhilRice advises plowing or rotovating 21 to 30 days before planting, then harrowing every 7 days. Other crops use shorter windows, so check the guide for your crop.

items.q: What is the difference between plowing and harrowing?
items.a: Plowing cuts and turns the soil, burying stubble and weeds. Harrowing breaks the clods and smooths the field, and it is repeated to level it.

items.q: Can I use a carabao instead of a tractor?
items.a: Yes. A UN CSAM review says the carabao with a native moldboard plow is still the main draft animal for rice and corn. It is slower, so it suits small plots.

items.q: Is zero tillage safe for corn?
items.a: A Bukidnon study found zero and minimum tillage matched conventional corn yields and saved cost and time. It used glyphosate on the weeds, and you must follow the FPA label.
